title: The Winter Trading Slump That's Quietly Eating Hospitality Margins
linkedin:
A 10% drop in winter covers rarely means a 10% drop in profit. For most hospitality businesses it is closer to 20 or 30%.

Here is why the gap opens.

Rosters get built around a busy trading pattern and rarely get revisited once the quiet months hit. A venue running 28 to 30% labour cost in summer can drift past 38 or 40% in winter without a single deliberate roster change. Nobody wants to be the one who trims a loyal team member's hours, so the roster keeps running as if trade never slowed.

Food cost percentage moves the same way, for a different reason. Winter menus lean into slow cooked, higher cost comfort dishes, and lower covers mean fresh stock turns over more slowly, so wastage creeps up. A dish sitting at 28% food cost in December can drift to 34 or 35% in winter, and most POS systems will not flag the shift on their own.

None of this needs a dramatic reset. It needs someone to actually sit with the winter numbers instead of waiting for spring trade to paper over them, which is hard to do from inside a business also running dinner service every night.

The quiet months are the best window all year to run a proper line by line look at cost and margin, precisely because trading volume is low enough that the review will not compete with a full house.

Cafe and restaurant owners: does your winter trade drop by 10% but your profit feel like it has dropped by double that?

You are probably right. Rosters and menus built for a busy trading period rarely get revisited once covers fall, so labour cost and food cost percentages quietly creep up while nobody is watching.

The fix is not a dramatic overhaul. It is usually one short, honest look at which shifts and which dishes are actually carrying their weight in the quiet months.

Winter is quiet for most Brisbane and Queensland cafes, restaurants and bars, and most owners plan for the revenue dip. What tends to surprise them is how much further profit falls behind it.

A 10% drop in covers often produces a 20 to 30% drop in profit, because rosters and menus built for busy season trade rarely get revisited once things quieten down. Labour cost as a share of takings and food cost percentage both tend to drift upward without anyone changing a single shift or dish on purpose.

The good news is that the quiet months are actually the easiest time of year to fix this. With lower trading volume, there is room to properly review which shifts and menu items are pulling their weight, rather than trying to do that work during a full house.

If you run a hospitality business on the east coast and winter numbers have felt harder to read than they should, it is worth a closer look before spring trade returns.
